Chapter 1: Understanding the Meantime—When Life Feels Uncertain
Have you ever felt like life just...hit pause? Like you’re stuck somewhere between what was and what’s next—where the past still echoes, but the future hasn’t quite shown up yet?
So many of us land in this in-between, often after a breakup, a disappointment, or some big change. The world seems to keep spinning, but inside, you’re just waiting—waiting for love, for clarity, maybe just for things to make sense again.
Now, this stretch of time—even though it can feel awkward or uncomfortable—isn’t wasted. It’s what some people call the “meantime.” And while it might seem like nothing’s happening, there’s actually a quiet transformation going on beneath the surface.
Think of the meantime as more than just a pause. It’s a space where old wounds come up, asking to be seen, and where the seeds of self-understanding start to take root.
Let me share a story. There was a woman who’d just ended a long relationship. Suddenly, her days felt empty. She tried to distract herself—throwing herself into work, meeting friends, even dating again—but nothing really worked. The loneliness stuck around, and she wondered... would she ever feel whole again?
It wasn’t until she stopped running from the discomfort that things shifted. She realized the meantime was actually nudging her to look inward—to finally face the parts of herself she’d been avoiding for years.
Most of us don’t even realize we’re in the meantime. We rush to fill the emptiness, hoping that something—anything—will make the pain vanish. But the meantime isn’t here to punish us or leave us stranded. It’s an invitation to slow down, to really listen.
It’s a chance to ask yourself, “What do I need to heal? What am I still carrying that’s weighing me down?”
During these periods, old memories have a way of bubbling up. There was a man, recently separated, who found himself thinking about childhood moments—times when he felt invisible or unworthy. At first, he tried to push these memories away, embarrassed by how persistent they were. But over time, he started to notice something: these memories were connected to patterns in his relationships. The meantime had given him space to see what he'd been avoiding.
It’s so easy to blame others for the pain that surfaces—to point fingers at ex-partners, parents, even fate. But the meantime gently nudges us to take a closer look. What part did I play in this? What can I learn from it?
And remember, this isn’t about beating yourself up. It’s about reclaiming your own power. The moment you start to see your role in your story, the meantime shifts—from just waiting, to actually growing.
For a lot of people, spirituality becomes a quiet companion during these times. Whether it’s turning to prayer, meditation, or just sitting in silence, there’s a sense that something bigger is at work—even if it’s tough to put into words.
In its own way, the meantime becomes sacred. It’s where healing quietly begins, and where the foundation for future love is gently laid.
